tool.name: Jupyter
tool.tagline: Interactive notebooks for code, results and narrative in one document
tool.description: Jupyter is the open-source platform behind notebooks: documents that mix live code, its output (tables, charts, widgets) and Markdown text. JupyterLab and Jupyter Notebook are the browser interfaces, kernels run the code (Python via IPython, and dozens of other languages), and tools like nbconvert and papermill turn notebooks into reports and pipelines. It is the default workspace for data analysis, teaching and research.

concepts.name: Notebooks, cells and execution order
concepts.summary: A notebook is a list of code and Markdown cells run by a kernel; outputs depend on the order you ran cells, not their position.
concepts.why: Every notebook surprise, from 'NameError' to stale results, comes from how cells and execution order work.
concepts.body:
A **notebook** (`.ipynb` file) is a sequence of **cells**. A **code cell** holds code that you run with Shift+Enter; its output (printed text, the value of the last expression, a chart, a table) appears right below it and is saved in the file. A **Markdown cell** holds formatted text, headings, lists, links and LaTeX math, so a notebook can read like a report.

Code runs in a separate process called the **kernel** (for Python, an IPython kernel). The kernel keeps one shared namespace for the whole notebook: a variable defined in one cell is visible in every other cell run afterwards.

The number in brackets, `[5]`, shows the order in which cells were executed. This order, not the position on the page, determines the kernel's state. You can run cell 7 and then cell 2, edit cell 2 and rerun it, or delete a cell whose variable still lives in memory. The result is **hidden state**: the notebook on screen no longer explains the results.

Habits that avoid trouble:

- Run cells top to bottom and keep the notebook runnable in that order.
- Before sharing, use **Restart Kernel and Run All Cells**; if anything fails, the notebook was relying on hidden state.
- Keep cells small and focused: load data, transform, plot.

Only the last expression of a cell is displayed automatically; use `print()` or `display()` for anything else.
concepts.code:
# Cell [1]
prices = [3.5, 4.0, 2.25]

# Cell [2]
total = sum(prices)
total                      # last expression is displayed: 9.75

# Cell [3] - later edited to: prices = [1, 2] and re-run
prices = [1, 2]

# Cell [2] is NOT re-run automatically, so `total` is stale:
print(total)               # 9.75, although sum(prices) is now 3
print(sum(prices))         # 3
# Fix: Kernel > Restart Kernel and Run All Cells
takeaways: Cells share one kernel namespace; execution order defines state
Only the last expression of a cell is shown automatically
Restart and Run All before trusting or sharing results
pitfalls: Deleting a cell and assuming its variables are gone; they live in the kernel until restart.

quiz.q: You ran cells in the order 1, 3, 2. What determines the values of variables now?
options: The order of cells on the page
The saved outputs in the file
quiz.explain: The kernel executes code in the order you ran it; position on the page does not matter.

concepts.name: Installing and launching JupyterLab
concepts.summary: Install JupyterLab or Notebook into an environment, start the server, and understand what runs where.
concepts.why: Setting Jupyter up per project avoids the classic 'module not found in the notebook' confusion.
concepts.body:
Jupyter has two main browser interfaces, both built on the same **Jupyter Server**:

- **JupyterLab**: a full workspace with a file browser, tabs, side-by-side notebooks, terminals and extensions.
- **Jupyter Notebook 7**: a simpler one-document-per-tab interface, built on JupyterLab components.

Install into the project's virtual environment so the notebook sees the same packages as your code:

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install jupyterlab
jupyter lab
```

`jupyter lab` (or `jupyter notebook`) starts a local web server, usually on `http://localhost:8888`, and opens your browser with a URL containing a **token**, a password that protects the server. The directory you start from becomes the root of the file browser. Stop the server with Ctrl+C in the terminal, or File > Shut Down.

Three pieces are now running: the server process in your terminal, the browser page that is only a front end, and a **kernel** process per open notebook that executes the code. Closing the browser tab does not stop kernels; use the Running panel to shut them down.

Editors also speak Jupyter: VS Code, PyCharm and others open `.ipynb` files directly and start kernels without a separate server, and hosted services such as Google Colab run notebooks in the cloud. The file format and kernels are the same everywhere.

`jupyter server list` shows running servers and their URLs if you lose the tab.
concepts.code:
# Per-project setup
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install jupyterlab pandas

jupyter lab --version              # 4.6.x
jupyter lab                        # opens http://localhost:8888/lab?token=...
jupyter lab --no-browser --port 8890   # e.g. on a remote machine

# In another terminal
jupyter server list                # running servers with their token URLs
takeaways: JupyterLab and Notebook 7 are front ends on the same Jupyter Server
Install Jupyter in the project environment, then run `jupyter lab`
Server, browser page and kernels are separate; closing a tab leaves kernels running
pitfalls: Installing Jupyter globally and the packages in a venv, so imports fail inside the notebook.

quiz.q: You close the browser tab of a running notebook. What happens to its kernel?
options: It keeps running until shut down or the server stops
It is converted to a script
quiz.explain: The browser is only a client; kernels live in the server and must be shut down explicitly.

concepts.name: Markdown and rich output
concepts.summary: Write formatted Markdown cells with math, and display tables, images, HTML and charts inline from code.
concepts.why: Rich output is what makes a notebook a readable analysis rather than a script with print statements.
concepts.body: **Markdown cells** support headings (`#`, `##`), bold and italic, lists, links, images, code blocks, tables and LaTeX math (`$E = mc^2$` inline, `$$...$$` on its own line). Press Shift+Enter to render, double-click to edit. Headings also build the table of contents panel in JupyterLab, which helps navigate long notebooks. **Code cells** display the value of their last expression using the richest format the object supports. That is why a pandas DataFrame appears as an HTML table and a Matplotlib or Plotly figure appears as a chart: the object offers HTML, PNG or JSON representations, and the front end picks the best one. To show more than the last expression, or to display from inside loops and functions, use `display()` (available automatically in notebooks, or from `IPython.display`). That module also has helpers: - `Markdown("**bold**")` and `HTML("bold")` render text you generate; - `Image("plot.png")` or `Image(url=...)`, `SVG`, `Video`, `Audio`; - `JSON(data)` for a collapsible tree in JupyterLab. End a line with `;` to suppress the display of its value, for example after a Matplotlib call that returns objects you do not want printed. Outputs are stored in the notebook file. Large images and HTML tables make files big and diffs noisy, so avoid printing huge DataFrames; `df.head()` or `df.sample(5)` is usually enough.
concepts.code:
from IPython.display import display, Markdown, HTML
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Oslo", "Lima"], "temp": [4.5, 19.0]})

display(Markdown(f"**{len(df)} cities**, warmest: *{df.loc[df.temp.idxmax(), 'city']}*"))
display(df)                        # rendered as an HTML table in a notebook
html = df.to_html(index=False)
display(HTML(html))

for city in df.city:
    display(Markdown(f"- {city}"))  # display works inside loops

df.temp.mean()                     # last expression is shown: 11.75
# In a notebook: Markdown/HTML render as formatted text; a plain
# Python shell prints their text fallback instead.
takeaways: Markdown cells give headings, lists, links and LaTeX math
The last expression is shown in its richest format; `display()` shows anything else
`IPython.display` has Markdown, HTML, Image, JSON and media helpers
pitfalls: Displaying an entire million-row DataFrame or huge images, bloating the saved notebook.

quiz.q: Inside a for loop you want each iteration to render a DataFrame as a table. What do you use?
options: Just write df on its own line
quiz.explain: Only a cell's last expression is auto-displayed; display() renders rich output from anywhere.

concepts.name: Command mode, edit mode and shortcuts
concepts.summary: Move between edit and command mode and use the core keyboard shortcuts to work quickly in notebooks.
concepts.why: A dozen shortcuts make notebook work several times faster than reaching for menus.
takeaways: Esc enters command mode, Enter enters edit mode
Shift+Enter runs and advances; A/B insert cells; D,D deletes; M/Y switch cell type
The command palette lists every action and shortcut
pitfalls: Typing while in command mode and accidentally deleting or converting cells; press Z to undo a deletion.

quiz.q: You are in command mode and press M. What happens?
options: The letter m is typed into the cell
The selected cell becomes a Markdown cell
The cell is merged with the next one
quiz.explain: In command mode M converts the selected cell to Markdown; Y converts it back to code.

concepts.name: Kernels and environments
concepts.summary: Understand what a kernel is, restart and interrupt it, and register virtual environments or other languages as kernels.
concepts.why: Picking the wrong kernel is the number one cause of 'it works in the terminal but not in the notebook'.
concepts.body:
A **kernel** is the process that runs a notebook's code and holds its variables. The front end sends code to it and receives outputs back. For Python the kernel is **ipykernel**, built on IPython; other kernels exist for R (IRkernel), Julia (IJulia), JavaScript, Rust, Go and many more.

Each kernel runs with one specific Python interpreter, and therefore one environment. A **kernelspec** (a small `kernel.json` file) tells Jupyter how to start it. To make a project's virtual environment available in a Jupyter installed elsewhere:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pip install ipykernel
.venv/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name myproj --display-name "Python (myproj)"
```

Then pick "Python (myproj)" from the kernel selector. `jupyter kernelspec list` shows registered kernels, and `jupyter kernelspec uninstall myproj` removes one. In a notebook, `import sys; sys.executable` tells you which interpreter is running.

Kernel controls:

- **Interrupt** (I, I or the stop button) raises `KeyboardInterrupt` in the running cell, useful for runaway loops.
- **Restart** clears all variables and imports; use it after upgrading a package or when state is confusing.
- If a kernel **dies** (often from running out of memory or a crashing C extension), all state is lost and you must rerun cells.

Install packages from a notebook with `%pip install package`: the magic always targets the kernel's own environment, unlike `!pip`, which may use a different pip on your PATH.
concepts.code:
# Register a project environment as a kernel
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -q ipykernel
.venv/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name myproj \
    --display-name "Python (myproj)"

jupyter kernelspec list
#   myproj     /home/me/.local/share/jupyter/kernels/myproj
#   python3    /usr/local/share/jupyter/kernels/python3

cat ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels/myproj/kernel.json
# {"argv": [".../.venv/bin/python", "-m", "ipykernel_launcher", "-f",
#   "{connection_file}"], "display_name": "Python (myproj)", "language": "python", ...}

jupyter kernelspec uninstall -y myproj
takeaways: A kernel is the process that executes code; each uses one interpreter and environment
Register environments with `python -m ipykernel install --user --name ...`
Use `%pip install` in notebooks so packages land in the kernel's environment
pitfalls: Running `!pip install` and installing into a different environment than the kernel uses.

quiz.q: A package imports fine in your terminal's venv but fails in the notebook. What should you check first?
options: Whether the notebook's kernel uses that venv's interpreter (sys.executable)
quiz.explain: The kernel decides the interpreter; if it is a different environment, the package is not installed there.

concepts.name: IPython magics and shell commands
concepts.summary: Use line and cell magics such as %timeit, %%time, %run, %pip and %autoreload, plus ! shell commands, from a notebook.
concepts.why: Magics give timing, profiling, reloading and shell access in one keyword, and appear constantly in notebooks you will read.
concepts.body:
The IPython kernel adds **magic commands** that are not Python syntax:

- **Line magics** start with `%` and apply to the rest of the line.
- **Cell magics** start with `%%`, must be the first line of a cell, and apply to the whole cell.

The ones you will use most:

- `%timeit expr` runs a statement many times and reports mean and spread; `%%timeit` times a cell.
- `%%time` (or `%time`) measures a single run, wall and CPU time.
- `%run script.py` runs a file in the notebook, leaving its variables available.
- `%pip install pkg` installs into the kernel's environment.
- `%load_ext autoreload` then `%autoreload 2` reloads edited modules before each cell, essential when developing a package alongside a notebook.
- `%matplotlib inline` or `%matplotlib widget` picks the plotting backend.
- `%who`, `%whos` list variables; `%env` reads or sets environment variables.
- `%%writefile file.py` saves the cell to a file; `%%bash` and `%%html` run or render other languages.
- `%debug` opens a debugger at the last exception; `%prun` profiles.

Lines starting with **`!`** run shell commands: `!ls data/`. The output can be captured into Python: `files = !ls *.csv`, and Python values interpolate with braces: `!echo {name}`.

`%lsmagic` lists all magics and `%timeit?` shows help. Magics only work in IPython-based kernels, so notebooks full of them do not run as plain `.py` scripts.
concepts.code:
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2

nums = list(range(10_000))
%timeit sum(nums)          # e.g. 290 µs ± 50 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, ...)
%time total = sum(x * x for x in nums)
print(total)               # 333283335000

name = "jupyter"
!echo hello {name}         # hello jupyter
files = !ls /
print(type(files).__name__, "usr" in files)   # SList True

%env APP_MODE=dev
import os
print(os.environ["APP_MODE"])                  # dev
takeaways: `%` line magics apply to one line; `%%` cell magics to the whole cell
%timeit/%%time for timing, %run for scripts, %autoreload for live module edits
`!cmd` runs shell commands; `x = !cmd` captures output, `{var}` interpolates
pitfalls: Putting a `%%` cell magic anywhere but the first line of the cell, which raises an error.

quiz.q: You edit a function in mymodule.py, but the notebook keeps using the old version after re-running `import mymodule`. What fixes this going forward?
quiz.explain: Python caches imported modules; autoreload re-imports changed modules before each cell executes.

concepts.name: Interactive widgets with ipywidgets
concepts.summary: Add sliders, dropdowns and buttons to notebooks with interact and ipywidgets, and react to changes with observe.
concepts.why: Widgets turn a notebook into a small exploratory app: tweak a parameter and see results update without editing code.
concepts.body:
**ipywidgets** provides interactive controls rendered in the notebook and synchronized with Python objects in the kernel. Install it in the kernel environment (`pip install ipywidgets`); JupyterLab 4 and Notebook 7 support it without extra steps.

The fastest route is `interact`, which builds controls from a function's arguments:

```python
from ipywidgets import interact
@interact(n=(1, 100), kind=["linear", "log"])
def show(n=10, kind="linear"): ...
```

A tuple becomes a slider, a list becomes a dropdown, a bool a checkbox, a string a text box. The function reruns every time a value changes; `interact_manual` adds a Run button for slow functions.

For more control, create widgets directly: `widgets.IntSlider(min=0, max=10)`, `Dropdown`, `Text`, `Button`, `Checkbox`, `DatePicker`, combined with layout containers `HBox`, `VBox`, `Tab` and `Accordion`. Each widget has a `value` trait. React to changes with:

- `w.observe(callback, names="value")`: called with a change dict holding `old` and `new`;
- `button.on_click(callback)`;
- `widgets.link((a, "value"), (b, "value"))` to keep two widgets in sync.

Printed output and plots from callbacks should go into a `widgets.Output()` area, used as a context manager, or they may vanish.

Widgets need a live kernel; in exported HTML they show their last state at best. For shareable apps, consider Voila, Streamlit or Dash.
concepts.code:
import ipywidgets as widgets

price = widgets.FloatSlider(value=10, min=0, max=50, step=0.5, description="Price")
qty = widgets.IntSlider(value=3, min=1, max=20, description="Qty")
total = widgets.Label()
log = []

def update(change=None):
    total.value = f"Total: {price.value * qty.value:.2f}"

price.observe(update, names="value")
qty.observe(update, names="value")
qty.observe(lambda ch: log.append((ch["old"], ch["new"])), names="value")
update()
ui = widgets.VBox([price, qty, total])     # display(ui) in a notebook

qty.value = 5                              # simulate the user moving a slider
print(total.value)                         # Total: 50.00
print(log)                                 # [(3, 5)]
takeaways: `interact` builds controls from function arguments in one line
Widgets have a `value`; react with `observe(..., names='value')` or `on_click`
Send callback output to a `widgets.Output()` area
pitfalls: Printing from a widget callback without an Output widget, so the output appears in the log instead of under the widget.

quiz.explain: interact turns a (min, max) tuple of ints into an IntSlider.

concepts.name: Working effectively in JupyterLab
concepts.summary: Use JupyterLab's file browser, side-by-side views, consoles, terminals, debugger, table of contents and extensions.
concepts.why: JupyterLab is a full workspace; using it as a single-notebook viewer leaves most of its productivity on the table.
concepts.body:
JupyterLab arranges documents and tools in tabs you can drag to split the main area, for example a notebook beside the CSV it reads, or two views of the same notebook.

Features worth knowing:

- **File browser** (left sidebar): open notebooks, CSV files (shown as a grid), images, Markdown with live preview, and text editors with syntax highlighting.
- **Consoles**: right-click a notebook and choose "New Console for Notebook" to get a scratch area attached to the same kernel, ideal for quick checks without cluttering the notebook.
- **Terminals**: a full shell in the browser, useful on remote servers.
- **Running panel**: lists open kernels and terminals so you can shut down forgotten ones holding memory.
- **Table of contents**: built from Markdown headings, for navigating long notebooks.
- **Debugger**: enable the bug icon on a notebook to set breakpoints by clicking line numbers, then inspect variables and the call stack (requires an ipykernel with debugger support, which current versions have).
- **Contextual help** (Ctrl+I) shows documentation for the object under the cursor.
- **Collapsible cells and outputs**, and "Render side-by-side" for long outputs.
- **Real-time collaboration** via the `jupyter-collaboration` extension.

**Extensions** add features such as Git integration (`jupyterlab-git`), language servers for completion and linting (`jupyterlab-lsp`) and formatters. In JupyterLab 4 most are installed with `pip`, with no build step; `jupyter labextension list` shows what is installed.
concepts.code:
jupyter lab --version                 # 4.6.x
jupyter labextension list             # installed front-end extensions

# Common extensions are plain pip packages in JupyterLab 4
pip install jupyterlab-git            # Git panel
pip install jupyterlab-lsp python-lsp-server   # completion, hover, linting
pip install jupyter-collaboration     # real-time collaboration

# Settings live in JSON and can be versioned per user
ls ~/.jupyter/lab/user-settings/@jupyterlab/
takeaways: Split the main area to work on several documents side by side
Attach a console to a notebook's kernel for scratch work
Use the Running panel, debugger and table of contents; add extensions with pip
pitfalls: Leaving many kernels running in the background, each holding data in memory.

quiz.q: You want to try quick expressions against a notebook's variables without adding cells to it. What do you use?
options: A console attached to the notebook's kernel
quiz.explain: A console for the notebook shares its kernel, so it sees the same variables without editing the document.

concepts.name: Exporting and executing notebooks
concepts.summary: Convert notebooks to HTML, PDF or scripts with nbconvert, and run them headless with parameters using papermill.
concepts.why: Notebooks become reports and scheduled jobs only when they can be executed and exported without a person clicking.
concepts.body:
**nbconvert** turns a notebook into other formats:

```bash
jupyter nbconvert --to html report.ipynb      # shareable, keeps outputs
jupyter nbconvert --to script analysis.ipynb  # .py file of the code cells
jupyter nbconvert --to webpdf report.ipynb    # PDF via a headless browser
```

`--execute` runs all cells top to bottom in a fresh kernel before converting, which both refreshes outputs and proves the notebook works from scratch. Add `--ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=600` for long cells, and `--no-input` to hide code and show only results, a common way to publish reports for non-programmers. `--to notebook --inplace --execute` updates the notebook itself.

**papermill** adds **parameters**: tag one cell `parameters` (cell toolbar > tags) containing defaults such as `region = "eu"`. Then

```bash
papermill report.ipynb out/report_us.ipynb -p region us -p year 2026
```

injects a new cell after it with the given values, executes the notebook and saves the result, with outputs, as a new notebook. Failed cells are highlighted in the output notebook, which makes it an excellent execution log. It also has a Python API, `papermill.execute_notebook`, useful in Airflow or other schedulers.

Under both tools sits **nbclient**, which starts a kernel and runs cells. For production pipelines, keep notebooks for exploration and reporting, and move reusable logic into importable `.py` modules that the notebook calls.
concepts.code:
# report.ipynb has a cell tagged "parameters": region = "eu"; year = 2025
jupyter nbconvert --to html --execute --no-input report.ipynb
#   [NbConvertApp] Writing ... bytes to report.html

jupyter nbconvert --to script report.ipynb       # -> report.py

papermill report.ipynb out/report_us.ipynb -p region us -p year 2026
#   Executing notebook with kernel: python3
#   (out/report_us.ipynb gets an injected cell: region = "us", year = 2026)

python - <<'EOF'
import papermill as pm
pm.execute_notebook("report.ipynb", "out/report_jp.ipynb",
                    parameters={"region": "jp"})
EOF
takeaways: `jupyter nbconvert --to html|script|webpdf` exports; `--execute` reruns first
`--no-input` publishes results without code
papermill injects parameters into a tagged cell and saves an executed copy
pitfalls: Exporting a notebook without `--execute`, shipping stale outputs that the current code would not produce.

quiz.q: How does papermill know where to inject `-p region us`?
options: It looks for a cell tagged 'parameters' and inserts a new cell after it
It edits every assignment to region
quiz.explain: papermill adds an injected-parameters cell right after the cell tagged parameters, overriding its defaults.

concepts.name: Reproducible notebooks and version control
concepts.summary: Avoid hidden state, pin environments, strip outputs, pair notebooks with scripts via Jupytext, and diff them with nbdime.
concepts.why: A notebook that only works on one person's machine, in one kernel session, is not a result anyone can trust.
concepts.body:
Reproducibility problems come from three sources: state, environment and files.

**State.** Out-of-order execution and deleted cells leave variables that the notebook no longer defines. Restart and Run All before sharing, and make CI run `jupyter nbconvert --execute` (or papermill) so broken notebooks fail fast. Set random seeds explicitly.

**Environment.** Record dependencies with pinned versions (`requirements.txt`, `uv.lock`, `environment.yml`) and use a dedicated kernel per project. Print key versions in the first cell when results matter, and avoid absolute paths to your home directory; use paths relative to the project.

**Files and Git.** `.ipynb` files are JSON that store outputs, execution counts and metadata, so diffs are noisy and images bloat history. Options:

- **nbstripout** installs a Git filter that removes outputs on commit (`nbstripout --install`).
- **Jupytext** pairs each notebook with a plain-text script, for example `py:percent` format with `# %%` cell markers. Review and diff the `.py` file; Jupytext keeps both in sync when you save. Many teams commit only the text version.
- **nbdime** provides notebook-aware `nbdiff` and `nbmerge`, and Git integration via `nbdime config-git --enable`.

Keep heavy logic in importable modules with tests, and let notebooks orchestrate and explain. A notebook that is mostly calls to well-named functions is easy to rerun, review and trust.
concepts.code:
# Pair a notebook with a percent-format script and keep them in sync
jupytext --set-formats ipynb,py:percent analysis.ipynb
jupytext --sync analysis.ipynb         # updates whichever is older
head -3 analysis.py
#   # ---
#   # jupyter:
#   #   jupytext:     (YAML header, then cells marked with # %%)

# Strip outputs automatically on commit
pip install nbstripout && nbstripout --install

# Notebook-aware diffs and merges in git
nbdime config-git --enable
git diff analysis.ipynb                # now shows cell-level changes

# Prove it runs from scratch (e.g. in CI)
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute analysis.ipynb --output /tmp/ci.ipynb
takeaways: Restart and Run All, and execute notebooks in CI to catch hidden state
Pin the environment and use relative paths and explicit seeds
Use nbstripout, Jupytext and nbdime to make notebooks Git-friendly
pitfalls: Committing notebooks with large outputs, so every rerun produces a huge, unreadable diff.

options: A paired .py script with `# %%` cell markers kept in sync with the notebook
quiz.explain: Jupytext pairs the notebook with a text representation that diffs and reviews cleanly.

concepts.name: The rich display protocol
concepts.summary: Make your own objects render nicely in notebooks with _repr_html_ and _repr_mimebundle_, and update outputs in place with display IDs.
concepts.why: Library authors and power users can give any object a table, chart or custom view in Jupyter with a single method.
concepts.body:
When a notebook displays an object, IPython asks it for representations in several **MIME types** and sends all of them to the front end, which chooses the richest it can render. An object opts in by defining methods:

- `_repr_html_()` returns HTML (pandas tables use this);
- `_repr_markdown_()`, `_repr_latex_()`, `_repr_svg_()`, `_repr_png_()`, `_repr_json_()`;
- `_repr_mimebundle_(include=None, exclude=None)` returns a dict mapping any MIME type to data, for full control, including custom types such as `application/vnd.plotly.v1+json`. Prefer either it or the individual methods, not both, so the result does not depend on how IPython combines them.

`__repr__` always provides the `text/plain` fallback, used in terminals and by front ends that understand nothing richer. The whole bundle is saved in the notebook, so the same output can appear as HTML in JupyterLab and as text in a terminal viewer.

Return `None` from a `_repr_*_` method to say "not available for this object", for example when it is too large to render.

**Display IDs** let you update an existing output instead of appending new ones:

```python
h = display("starting...", display_id=True)
h.update("50% done")
```

Every output with that display ID updates, which is perfect for progress messages or live-updating results.

For types you do not own, register a formatter: `get_ipython().display_formatter.formatters["text/html"].for_type(MyType, func)`.
concepts.code: from IPython import get_ipython # run this in a notebook kernel from IPython.display import display class Money: def __init__(self, amount, currency): self.amount, self.currency = amount, currency def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.amount}, {self.currency!r})" def _repr_html_(self): color = "green" if self.amount >= 0 else "red" return f"{self.amount:,.2f} {self.currency}" def _repr_markdown_(self): return f"**{self.amount:,.2f} {self.currency}**" m = Money(-1234.5, "EUR") data, meta = get_ipython().display_formatter.format(m) print(sorted(data)) # ['text/html', 'text/markdown', 'text/plain'] print(data["text/plain"]) # Money(-1234.5, 'EUR') h = display("step 1 of 3", display_id=True) # in a notebook: one output h.update("step 3 of 3") # ...updated in place
takeaways: IPython collects a bundle of MIME representations; the front end picks the richest
Define `_repr_html_` or `_repr_mimebundle_` to give objects a rich view
`display(..., display_id=True)` returns a handle whose `update()` edits output in place
pitfalls: Returning enormous HTML from `_repr_html_`, which slows the browser and bloats saved notebooks.

quiz.q: Your object defines both `__repr__` and `_repr_html_`. What does JupyterLab show?
options: An error: only one is allowed
The HTML representation, with text/plain kept as a fallback
quiz.explain: All representations are sent; JupyterLab renders the richest it supports, which is HTML.

concepts.name: The .ipynb format and nbformat
concepts.summary: Read, create, validate and execute notebooks programmatically using the nbformat JSON schema and nbclient.
concepts.why: Tooling such as linters, report generators, graders and migration scripts all work by manipulating notebook JSON.
concepts.code:
import nbformat
from nbformat.v4 import new_notebook, new_code_cell, new_markdown_cell
from nbclient import NotebookClient

nb = new_notebook()
nb.cells = [
    new_markdown_cell("# Generated report"),
    new_code_cell("x = 21\nx * 2"),
    new_code_cell("print('done')", metadata={"tags": ["remove-input"]}),
]
nbformat.validate(nb)                       # raises if the schema is violated
NotebookClient(nb, timeout=60, kernel_name="python3").execute()

out = nb.cells[1].outputs[0]
print(out.output_type, out.data["text/plain"])   # execute_result 42
print(nb.cells[2].outputs[0].text.strip())       # done
print(nb.nbformat, nb.nbformat_minor >= 5, len(nb.cells[1].id) > 0)  # 4 True True
nbformat.write(nb, "report.ipynb")
takeaways: A notebook is JSON: cells with source, metadata and outputs, plus notebook metadata
Outputs are stream, execute_result, display_data or error objects with MIME bundles
Use nbformat to read, build and validate notebooks and nbclient to execute them
pitfalls: Editing notebook JSON by hand with string operations and producing files that fail schema validation.

quiz.q: Where is a cell's chart image stored in an executed .ipynb file?
options: As a base64 string in the cell's outputs (a display_data MIME bundle)
Nowhere; it is regenerated on open
quiz.explain: Rich outputs are saved inline as MIME bundles, images base64 encoded, which is why files grow.

concepts.name: Kernel architecture and the messaging protocol
concepts.summary: See how front ends talk to kernels over ZeroMQ channels with the Jupyter messaging protocol, and drive a kernel from Python with jupyter_client.
concepts.why: Understanding the protocol explains kernel behavior (busy/idle, interrupts, stray output) and lets you build tools that run code in kernels.
takeaways: Kernels speak a JSON messaging protocol over ZeroMQ channels: shell, iopub, stdin, control, heartbeat
Outputs are linked to requests through `parent_header.msg_id`
`jupyter_client` starts kernels and sends requests from Python
pitfalls: Assuming outputs arrive on the shell channel; results and prints are broadcast on iopub.

quiz.q: On which channel does a client receive printed output and the busy/idle status of a kernel?
quiz.explain: iopub broadcasts side effects such as stream output, display data, results and status to all clients.

concepts.name: Server security and multi-user deployment
concepts.summary: Run Jupyter safely on remote machines with tokens, passwords, TLS and SSH tunnels, and serve teams with JupyterHub.
concepts.why: A Jupyter server executes arbitrary code as its user, so an exposed or misconfigured server is a full remote shell for an attacker.
concepts.body:
A running Jupyter Server can execute any code with the permissions of the user who started it. Treat access to it like SSH access.

**Authentication.** By default the server generates a random **token** and only listens on `localhost`. Keep both defaults whenever possible. Set a hashed password with `jupyter server password`, which writes it to the config directory. Never run with an empty token on a reachable interface, and avoid `--allow-root` outside containers.

**Remote machines.** The safest pattern is to keep the server on localhost and tunnel:

```bash
ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 user@gpu-box
```

then open `http://localhost:8888` locally. If you must listen on a network interface (`--ip 0.0.0.0`), put it behind TLS (`--certfile`, `--keyfile`, or a reverse proxy) and a strong password or token.

**Configuration** lives in `jupyter_server_config.py` (generate with `jupyter server --generate-config`) using traitlets: `c.ServerApp.ip`, `c.ServerApp.port`, `c.ServerApp.root_dir`, `c.IdentityProvider.token`. Every option can also be passed on the command line, such as `--ServerApp.port=9000`. `jupyter --paths` shows where configs, data and runtime files live.

**Teams.** **JupyterHub** runs a hub that authenticates users (OAuth, LDAP, GitHub ...) and spawns a separate single-user server per person, on one machine, in Docker containers, or on Kubernetes (Zero to JupyterHub with Helm). Resource limits, idle culling and shared storage are configured at the hub level.

Remember that notebooks can contain malicious code or outputs; Jupyter marks notebooks as untrusted and disables JavaScript outputs until you trust them.
concepts.code:
# Remote GPU box: keep the server on localhost and tunnel to it
ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 me@gpu-box
jupyter lab --no-browser --port 8888       # run on gpu-box (listens on localhost)

# Set a password instead of copying tokens around
jupyter server password                    # stores a hashed password

# Generate and edit the config file
jupyter server --generate-config           # ~/.jupyter/jupyter_server_config.py
cat >> ~/.jupyter/jupyter_server_config.py <<'EOF'
c.ServerApp.ip = "127.0.0.1"
c.ServerApp.root_dir = "/srv/projects"
c.ServerApp.open_browser = False
EOF

jupyter --paths                            # config, data and runtime locations
# Teams: JupyterHub spawns one server per user (pip install jupyterhub)
takeaways: A Jupyter server runs arbitrary code as its user: protect it like SSH
Keep localhost and tokens; use SSH tunnels or TLS plus passwords for remote access
Configure via traitlets (`c.ServerApp...`); use JupyterHub for multi-user setups
pitfalls: Starting `jupyter lab --ip 0.0.0.0` with an empty token on a cloud VM, exposing a remote shell to the internet.

quiz.q: You need to use Jupyter on a remote server from your laptop. What is the safest common setup?
options: Run with --ip 0.0.0.0 and no token for convenience
Disable authentication and rely on an unusual port
Keep the server on localhost and connect through an SSH tunnel
quiz.explain: An SSH tunnel keeps the server unreachable from the network while you access it securely.
